title: Applying plures contra Herculem. A commentary on ‘New intrageneric interactions in Macroptilium (Benth.)’
content: Modern cytomolecular approaches provide comprehensive insights into various aspects of plant nuclear genome organization, including comparative analyses of individual chromosomes, as well as the structure and evolution of entire chromosome complements in related species (for a recent review, see Wolny et al., 2025). Such karyotype-oriented studies rely heavily on fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) probes derived from unique or low-copy sequences that span relatively large chromosomal regions. These sequences are sufficiently conserved to serve as chromosome-specific landmarks among closely related taxa, thereby enabling comparative chromosome painting (CCP) and comparative chromosome barcoding (CCB). Various limitations linked to genomic repeat content and to the construction and maintenance of large-insert genomic libraries (e.g. Bacterial Artificial Chromosome libraries) have historically confined the application of CCP and CCB to a few small-genome model species and their close relatives (e.g. Lysak et al., 2006). This changed when Han et al. (2015) used synthesized oligonucleotide libraries to develop probes, initiating the use of oligo-FISH in plants. Combined with the rapidly increasing availability of sequenced plant nuclear genomes (Schwacke et al., 2025), this innovation has transformed analyses of chromosome and karyotype evolution on an unprecedented scale (Wolny et al., 2025). Although such analyses alone might not be sufficient to resolve definitely complex phylogenetic relationships among closely related species or the evolution of their karyotypes, they often provide valuable evidence that can support or challenge existing classifications, particularly when integrated with genomic or other omics data, morphological characters, embryological features and palynological evidence.
